intro: The three representative emergencies on the ISS are fire, rapid depressurization, and toxic atmosphere (such as ammonia). Alarms are not about mood; they initiate a sequence of isolation, respiration, reporting, and fire suppression or repair.
lessons.0.title: Three emergencies, different sounds, same priorities
lessons.0.summary: Life, vehicle controllability, mission. Trying to fix everything at once delays everything.
lessons.0.body.0: Official candidate training includes emergency procedures, maintenance, and repair in basic training. Representative scenarios repeatedly practiced in the U.S. segment of the ISS include fire, rapid depressurization, and toxic atmosphere. Ammonia appears as a leak in the external thermal control system; if it enters the cabin, it immediately threatens the respiratory system and eyes.
lessons.0.body.1: The three have different symptoms: smoke and heat, wind and ear popping, and irritating odors and coughing. However, the first actions are common. Can you breathe? Where is the crew member next to you? Which hatch do you close to isolate the system? What one sentence do you send to Houston?
lessons.0.body.2: The minigame requires selecting the correct response within a time limit. Speed is not about skipping steps, but about discarding items that cause hesitation.
lessons.0.facts.0.label: Representative
lessons.0.facts.1.label: First
lessons.0.deepDive.title: Distinguishing alarm types from confirmed facts
lessons.0.deepDive.body.0: A key learning point is to report the hypothesis indicated by an alarm separately from the state confirmed by measurements or visual inspection. For fire, pressure loss, and hazardous substances, the objects to protect and the methods of protection differ. Do not apply a response learned for one alarm to a different event without evidence.
lessons.0.deepDive.body.1: Options in the game are short decision examples for learning principles. Actual fault isolation, isolation, and evacuation require the status of equipment and procedures established by the responsible personnel. In the review, organize what is known, what is unconfirmed, and who to inform.
lessons.1.title: The alarm panel does not tell a story. It points to systems.
lessons.1.summary: Sounds and lights only convey which detector, in which module, saw what.
lessons.1.body.0: Cabin alarms are distinguished by tone and display for fire, depressurization, toxic substances, and system anomalies. Training teaches: do not create a story from the sound. First, read the display and state which compartment's detector triggered the alarm. Even for a false alarm, do not return to normal operations until confirmation is complete.
lessons.1.body.1: Official fire protection explanations list detection, suppression, protective equipment, and post-event monitoring as design requirements. The alarm is the first switch in that chain. It is not the job to turn it off and silence it.
lessons.1.body.2: Ground control sees the same alarms via telemetry. Before CAPCOM says 'we see it too,' the crew adds the smell and sound from the scene. Report only information not available to sensors, briefly.
lessons.1.facts.0.label: Read
lessons.1.facts.1.label: Do Not
lessons.2.title: Fire in microgravity does not go up
lessons.2.summary: Flames are nearly spherical, and smoke follows ventilation flow. Fire suppression requires abandoning gravity-based common sense.
lessons.2.body.0: OCHMO fire protection explanations emphasize that historical combustion events and the inhalation of combustion products immediately threaten life. There is little room to escape, and the atmosphere is fragile. The greatest protection is prevention—selection of fire-resistant materials—and once it occurs, detection, suppression, protection, and purification are a set.
lessons.2.body.1: NASA-STD-3001 requires that extinguishers are quickly reachable and can target both open spaces and behind panels. In microgravity, extinguishing agents do not fall 'down.' Aim the nozzle at the source, stop ventilation, and cut the path of fire spread. PPE is worn near smoke or before entering. Even small amounts of combustion products can be immediately harmful.
lessons.2.body.2: The real work begins after the fire is out. Monitor the atmosphere, run filters, and watch for re-ignition. Official guidelines state that the fire suppression system itself must not create new hazards. The choice of water or foam is a judgment that considers both electrical systems and life support simultaneously.
lessons.2.facts.0.label: First
lessons.2.facts.1.label: If It Occurs
lessons.2.facts.1.value: PPE, Stop Ventilation, Aim at Source
lessons.3.title: Rapid depressurization is determined by the order of closing, not the size of the hole
lessons.3.summary: Ears, wind, and alarms arrive simultaneously. First, respiration and communication, then isolate the leaking compartment.
lessons.3.body.0: Loss of pressurization varies in scale from tiny holes to hatch failures to impacts. Small leaks can be isolated by observing which module's pressure is dropping. For large holes, oxygen and time calculations come first; if repair cannot be completed in time, evacuate.
lessons.3.body.1: Hatches can be allies or enemies when closed. Closing the wrong hatch can trap you on the side of fire or poison, or cut off the main line of life support. This is where the reason for learning coupling diagrams in ISS system courses pays off.
lessons.3.body.2: Communication is short. 'Depressurization, [Module Name], closing hatch, [Number] people.' Ground control can calculate the leak rate and the next valve to close. Speculative stories waste time.
lessons.3.facts.0.label: Minor Leak
lessons.3.facts.1.label: Major Breach
lessons.4.title: Ammonia is a cooling liquid and an asphyxiating gas
lessons.4.summary: When external thermal control leaks enter the cabin, masks and isolation may take precedence over fire suppression.
lessons.4.body.0: External thermal control circulates ammonia. Official EVA anomaly logs record ammonia exposure from cooling line disconnection, crystal formation on suits, and sunlit bakeout. Symptoms include rhinorrhea, sore throat, chest tightness, cough, dyspnea, and eye irritation; heavy exposure can cause severe respiratory distress and burns.
lessons.4.body.1: The protocol for cabin entry involves donning masks (PPE), isolating the leaking system, sealing the contaminated compartment, and evacuating to a separate atmosphere, such as the Russian segment, if necessary. Running ventilation indiscriminately can spread the toxin throughout the entire spacecraft.
lessons.4.body.2: Bringing crystals from EVA into the cabin falls under the same protocol. Quest bakeout and detector verification are conditions for opening the hatch. Rushing inside can create a secondary incident.
lessons.4.facts.0.label: Source
lessons.4.facts.1.label: Protocol
lessons.5.title: Cabin modules are corridors and traps
lessons.5.summary: Smoke and toxins ride the ventilation; airflow indicates the direction of leaks. Cut off the path of travel first.
lessons.5.body.0: CO2 and fire byproducts studied in closed-environment medicine become physical realities here. Ventilation fans normally mix air but can transport contamination during emergencies. Official fire guidelines require the ability to extinguish fires behind panels. Do not chase only visible flames.
lessons.5.body.1: Establish a muster point. Assign who holds the extinguisher, who distributes masks, and who communicates with the ground. Role declarations practiced in T-38 and survival training are effective in narrow cylindrical spaces.
lessons.5.body.2: Even if lighting and visibility drop, the body should remember the location of handrails and hatches. NBL and module identification support movement under emergency lighting.
lessons.5.facts.0.label: Ventilation
lessons.5.facts.1.label: Personnel
lessons.6.title: Hatches are mechanical open/close devices and declarations of boundaries
lessons.6.summary: The moment a hatch closes, it determines which atmosphere is protected. Do not skip equalization and leak checks.
lessons.6.body.0: Node hatches separate laboratories, airlocks, visiting vehicles, and the Russian segment. The series configuration of equipment and crew locks seen in Quest training also serves as isolation training for emergencies. Opening without equalizing pressure can damage ears, lungs, and coupling mechanisms.
lessons.6.body.1: Whether pressure recovers after closing provides evidence of the leak location. If it does not recover, the closed boundary is incorrect or there are multiple leaks. Do not close the next hatch without evidence.
lessons.6.body.2: Emergencies during visiting vehicle docking require monitoring both CBM and arm status simultaneously. The 'Stop' command from robotics training is also correct here.
lessons.6.facts.0.label: Before Opening
lessons.6.facts.1.label: After Closing
lessons.7.title: What is passed to Houston is a state vector, not a novel
lessons.7.summary: What, where, who, what was done, what is needed next. If five words suffice, five words are enough.
lessons.7.body.0: CAPCOM, learned in control training, is a single voice. If everyone jumps into the loop during an emergency, the room becomes blind. The same applies on the spacecraft; fix the speaking role to one person.
lessons.7.body.1: Official candidate experiences include joining an MCC shift to observe a day on the watching side. Those who know they will one day sit in the seat receiving short reports do not send long excuses.
lessons.7.body.2: Even if communication is lost, procedures continue. The protocol for sharing the next action before LOS (Loss of Signal) applies here. Upon reconnection, do not fill gaps with speculation; resynchronize pressure, CO2, and headcount.
lessons.7.facts.0.label: One Sentence
lessons.7.facts.1.label: Interruption
lessons.8.title: Time limits are not cruelty, but physiology
lessons.8.summary: Oxygen, pressure, toxicity, heat. All run out before the length of a discussion.
lessons.8.body.0: Time limits in mini-games are not just for entertainment tension. Decompression time remaining, mask capacity, fire oxygen supply, and ammonia diffusion progress in real time. Official fire guidelines make 'extinguishing within required time' a design condition for this reason.
lessons.8.body.1: When discussions drag on, designate a lead. T-38 CRM and Flight Control use the same model. Dissenting opinions should be stated in one sentence, accompanied by an alternative and required time.
lessons.8.body.2: A decision made when time runs out is a decision to survive, not a perfect decision. Post-event debriefs allow for approaching perfection in the next simulation.
lessons.8.facts.0.label: Depleting Factors
lessons.8.facts.1.label: Technique
lessons.9.title: After the calm, medicine and prevention remain
lessons.9.summary: Even after extinguishing the fire, sealing the hole, and cutting off the toxin, lungs, eyes, and records remain.
lessons.9.body.0: Fire prevention guidelines include post-incident cleanup and monitoring as design requirements. The EVA anomaly log specifically documents respiratory symptoms following ammonia exposure. Provide the surgeon with exposure duration, symptoms, and whether protective equipment was worn. Enduring discomfort is not a substitute for missing data.
lessons.9.body.1: Preventing recurrence requires identifying whether the material, connector, or procedure failed. A spacecraft must not accept the same event as 'familiarity.'
lessons.9.body.2: This module's badge certifies the ability to identify three types of emergencies within a time limit. In the final control integration exercise, translate these same types into the room's verbal communication.
lessons.9.facts.0.label: Medicine
lessons.9.facts.1.label: Operations
quiz.0.prompt: Which three representative emergencies are repeatedly trained in the U.S. segment of the ISS?
quiz.0.explanation: Fire, loss of pressure, and toxic atmospheres (such as ammonia) are treated as the three pillars that directly threaten life.
quiz.1.prompt: What does the official fire protection guide emphasize as the primary defense?
quiz.1.explanation: OCHMO-TB-008 states that the primary fire protection approach for current crewed vehicles is prevention.
quiz.2.prompt: What does the official protocol require before approaching smoke or entering that environment?
quiz.2.explanation: Even small amounts of combustion byproducts can be immediately harmful, so PPE must be worn before approaching.
quiz.3.prompt: What is the representative toxic substance involved in ISS external thermal control leaks?
quiz.3.explanation: The external cooling loop uses ammonia; contamination inside the cabin or suit threatens the respiratory system and eyes.
quiz.4.prompt: What is the official recorded response to ammonia crystals on a suit?
quiz.4.choices.0: Bakeout using sunlight to evaporate them
quiz.4.choices.1: Washing with water and entering the cabin directly
quiz.4.explanation: Records such as STS-98 indicate that bakeout using sunlight to evaporate crystals was used for decontamination.
quiz.5.prompt: What is the appropriate first response to a small pressurization leak?
quiz.5.choices.1: Identifying the section with dropping pressure and isolating it
quiz.5.explanation: Identify which module's pressure is dropping, close the hatch, and contain the leak.
quiz.6.prompt: What should be read first when an alarm sounds?
quiz.6.choices.2: The type of alarm and which section's detector triggered it
quiz.6.explanation: Do not create a narrative from the sound alone; first identify the system and section indicated. Do not return to normal operations before confirmation.
quiz.7.prompt: Which option aligns with the requirements of NASA-STD-3001 regarding fire extinguishers?
quiz.7.choices.1: Ensuring they work only in the direction of gravity
quiz.7.choices.3: Ensuring quick access and the ability to extinguish fires in open spaces and behind panels
quiz.7.explanation: Design requires quick access and the ability to extinguish fires in open spaces and behind panels, without creating new hazards.
quiz.8.prompt: What is the skeleton of the information to be passed to Houston during an emergency?
quiz.8.choices.0: What / Where / Who / What was done / What is needed
quiz.8.explanation: CAPCOM is a single voice; the shorter and more aligned the state vector, the more effectively the room can act.
quiz.9.prompt: What is the appropriate understanding of ventilation fans during an emergency?
quiz.9.choices.0: Always running at maximum is correct
quiz.9.choices.1: They can also transport contamination, so stop them or choose the direction
quiz.9.choices.3: They are another name for fire extinguishers
quiz.9.explanation: In daily operations, they mix air; in emergencies, they can spread smoke or toxins. Handling differs for fire versus toxins.
quiz.10.prompt: What is required before opening a hatch?
quiz.10.explanation: Opening without equalizing pressure damages ears, lungs, and joint mechanisms. After closing, confirm the leak location by pressure recovery.
quiz.11.prompt: What does this module cite as the basis for time limits?
quiz.11.choices.3: Physiology and physics such as oxygen, pressure, toxicity, and heat
quiz.11.explanation: Just as fire guidelines make 'extinguishing within required time' a design condition, the environment fails before debate can conclude.
quiz.12.prompt: Which symptoms are included in the official list of ammonia exposure effects?
quiz.12.choices.0: Rhinorrhea, sore throat, chest tightness, cough, dyspnea, eye irritation
quiz.12.explanation: The EVA anomaly log lists rhinorrhea, scratchy throat, chest tightness, cough, dyspnea, and eye irritation.
quiz.13.prompt: What is likely to happen if one tries to fix everything simultaneously in a complex emergency?
quiz.13.choices.0: Everything is fixed in the shortest time
quiz.13.choices.1: Everything is delayed, and life priority is buried
quiz.13.explanation: Prioritize life, then the vehicle, then the mission. Simultaneous repair is not feasible without a lead.
quiz.14.prompt: Which of the following is the appropriate medical information to retain after suppression?
quiz.14.choices.0: A single statement that one feels well
quiz.14.choices.2: Exposure duration, symptoms, and presence of protective equipment
quiz.14.choices.3: A promotional draft for the next day
quiz.14.explanation: Both fire combustion products and ammonia require specific exposure data for post-incident monitoring and the surgeon.
quiz.15.prompt: Which decision is appropriate when a large breach cannot be repaired in time?
quiz.15.choices.1: Close incorrect hatches one after another
quiz.15.choices.3: Calculate the time available and evacuate if necessary
quiz.15.explanation: A large breach becomes a matter of oxygen and time. Maintain an evacuation threshold while attempting isolation.
glossary.0.description: Rapid loss of pressurization. Addressed by managing leak rates and compartment isolation, or evacuation if isolation is not feasible.
glossary.1.description: Cabin contamination from substances such as ammonia or combustion products that threaten the respiratory system and eyes. PPE and isolation take priority.
glossary.2.description: Decontamination process that vaporizes ammonia crystals on suits using sunlight to prevent contamination inside the cabin.
glossary.3.description: Masks, respirators, etc. Must be worn before entering areas near smoke or toxic substances.
glossary.4.description: Cabin alarm system that signals fires, decompression, or system anomalies via audio and visual indicators.
glossary.5.description: Closing hatches to contain contamination or leaks in a specific section, allowing the remaining main sections to remain habitable.
glossary.6.description: Secondary hazards from fires. In a closed atmosphere, even small amounts can be immediately harmful.
glossary.7.description: Equalizing pressure on both sides of a hatch before opening. Skipping this step can damage ears, lungs, and mechanical components.
